descriptions:
Your short Moroccan journey starts with a full guided day in Marrakech, at a gentle pace. Meet your licensed local guide at your riad and walk to the Koutoubia, the 12th-century mosque whose minaret is the city's landmark, then continue to the Bahia Palace, a 19th-century residence of carved cedar ceilings, painted doors and tiled courtyards full of orange trees.

Late morning, visit the Saadian Tombs, the richly decorated burial place of a 16th-century dynasty, then dive into the souks, where your guide shows you how the markets are organised by trade and how bargaining works. Stop for lunch wherever you like; your guide knows good places for a tagine or a simple salad in a quiet courtyard.

In the afternoon your driver takes you to the Majorelle Garden, the cobalt-blue villa and cactus garden restored by Yves Saint Laurent, a calm green break from the medina. End the day at Jemaa el-Fna as the food stalls light up and the musicians gather.

GOOD TO KNOW
• Majorelle uses timed tickets sold online; book a day ahead to avoid the queue.
• Wear comfortable shoes: the medina is visited on foot.
• In the souks, a first price is an opening offer; your guide can help you agree a fair one.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
09:00 – Koutoubia and Bahia Palace
11:00 – Saadian Tombs
12:00 – Souks
13:30 – Lunch (not included)
15:00 – Majorelle Garden
17:00 – Jemaa el-Fna

INCLUDED: licensed guide and driver, riad night with breakfast.
NOT INCLUDED: entrance fees, lunch, tips.

Overnight: Marrakech (riad)
Meals: breakfast

Leave the heat and bustle of Marrakech behind and drive about 90 minutes south into the High Atlas. The road follows the Asni valley, past Berber villages, walnut groves and terraced fields, to Imlil, a mountain village at about 1,740 m at the foot of Jbel Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak (4,167 m).

In Imlil you meet a local mountain guide for a walk through the valley: up through the apple and cherry orchards, along irrigation channels and across streams, to the village of Aroumd, where houses of stone and earth cling to the slope. The walk is easy to moderate, about 3 to 4 hours with breaks, and your guide adapts the route to your pace. Along the way you stop for mint tea in a village home and learn about daily life in the mountains: farming, weaving and the weekly souk.

In the late afternoon, check in to your guesthouse. Evenings are quiet and cool; dinner, usually a tagine or couscous cooked in the guesthouse kitchen, is served with views of the peaks as the light fades.

GOOD TO KNOW
• Bring walking shoes with good grip, a warm layer and a hat; it's often 10 °C cooler than in Marrakech.
• Pack a small overnight bag; mules can carry luggage to guesthouses that cars can't reach.
• Guesthouses are simple and comfortable; heating may be basic in winter, and blankets are provided.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
09:00 – Depart Marrakech
10:30 – Imlil
11:00 – Walk with a mountain guide, mint tea in a village home
13:00 – Lunch (not included)
17:00 – Guesthouse

INCLUDED: vehicle and driver, mountain guide, guesthouse with dinner and breakfast.
NOT INCLUDED: lunch, tips.

Overnight: Imlil (mountain guesthouse)
Meals: breakfast and dinner

Wake to the sound of the mountains and breakfast on the guesthouse terrace with views of the Toubkal massif. Then leave the Atlas and drive west across the Haouz plain and the argan country towards the Atlantic, about four hours with stops.

On the way, stop at a women's argan oil cooperative, where you see how the nuts are cracked by hand, roasted and pressed into cooking oil and cosmetic oil. Argan trees grow only in this corner of Morocco; you may see goats climbing in their branches near the road, a famous sight, although some are placed there by herders for photos and expect a tip.

You reach Essaouira in the early afternoon. This fortified port town, listed by UNESCO, has a relaxed medina of white walls and blue shutters, built in the 18th century and designed by a French engineer. Check in to your riad, then walk along the Skala de la Ville, the sea ramparts lined with old bronze cannons, and watch the sunset over the Atlantic. Dinner is free tonight: Essaouira is known for its grilled fish.

GOOD TO KNOW
• Essaouira is windy most of the year; bring a windproof layer, even in summer.
• At the cooperative there is no obligation to buy; the oil is genuine and fairly priced.
• The medina is small and easy to explore on foot, and calmer than Marrakech.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
09:00 – Depart Imlil
13:00 – Argan cooperative
14:30 – Essaouira, check in
17:30 – Sea ramparts at sunset

INCLUDED: vehicle and driver, riad night with breakfast.
NOT INCLUDED: lunch, dinner, drinks, tips.

Overnight: Essaouira (riad)
Meals: breakfast

Spend the morning in Essaouira before heading back to Marrakech. Start early at the fishing port, where blue wooden boats unload the night's catch, gulls circle overhead and boat builders work on new hulls by hand, as they have for generations. You can choose your own fish and have it grilled at one of the stalls by the harbour.

Then walk through the medina: the woodworkers' workshops under the ramparts, known for their inlaid thuya wood, the spice market and the art galleries. Essaouira has inspired musicians and artists for decades, and in June it hosts the Gnaoua World Music Festival. If you prefer the beach, the long sandy bay south of the town is ideal for a walk or a camel ride along the shore.

After lunch, your driver takes you back to Marrakech, about three hours by road, and drops you at your hotel, riad or the airport in the late afternoon.

GOOD TO KNOW
• Fresh fish at the port is sold by weight; agree the price, including grilling, before ordering.
• Thuya wood boxes and trays make good, light souvenirs.
• If you fly home today, choose an evening flight from Marrakech.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates)
09:00 – Fishing port and ramparts
10:30 – Medina, woodworkers and spice market
12:00 – Lunch (not included)
13:00 – Depart
16:00 – Marrakech

INCLUDED: vehicle and driver, drop-off in Marrakech.
NOT INCLUDED: lunch, drinks, tips.

Overnight: not included (end of the tour)
Meals: breakfast

faq.question: Does this 4-day tour include the Sahara desert?
faq.answer: No. This trip focuses on mountains and ocean instead of long desert drives: Marrakech, the High Atlas around Imlil and the Atlantic town of Essaouira. The longest drive is about four hours. If you'd like to see the dunes, look at our desert tours from Marrakech, or ask us to combine both in a longer trip.

faq.question: Is this a private tour?
faq.answer: Yes. Only you and the people you book with travel in the vehicle, with your own driver for the four days, a licensed guide in Marrakech and a mountain guide in Imlil. You choose the start date, and the pace adapts to you. There is no minimum group size.

faq.question: Which meals are included?
faq.answer: Breakfast every day, and dinner at the mountain guesthouse in Imlil, where there are no restaurants nearby. Lunches, the dinners in Marrakech and Essaouira, and drinks are not included, so you can try the many local restaurants; Essaouira is famous for its grilled fish.

faq.question: How hard is the walk in the High Atlas?
faq.answer: It's an easy to moderate walk of about 3 to 4 hours with breaks, on village paths with some ups and downs, at around 1,700–2,000 m. No mountaineering experience is needed, just reasonable fitness and good shoes. Your mountain guide adapts the route to your group, and it can be shortened for children or older travellers.

faq.question: Where do we sleep?
faq.answer: Night 1 in a riad in Marrakech, night 2 in a mountain guesthouse in Imlil, and night 3 in a riad in Essaouira's medina. You choose the level when you book: comfortable hotels and riads, or charming riads and boutique hotels. The Imlil guesthouse is simpler and cosy, with mountain views.

faq.question: Can we see Mount Toubkal?
faq.answer: Yes. Imlil is the starting point for Toubkal, North Africa's highest peak (4,167 m), and on clear days the summit area is visible from the valley. This tour doesn't climb it; reaching the summit needs two days and good fitness. If you'd like to try, ask us to plan a Toubkal trek.

faq.question: What should I pack?
faq.answer: Comfortable walking shoes with good grip, a warm layer for the mountain evening, a windproof jacket for Essaouira, sun cream, sunglasses and a hat. A small overnight bag is useful for Imlil. In winter, bring warmer clothes: the Atlas can be cold and occasionally snowy.

faq.question: When is the best time for this tour?
faq.answer: It works all year. Spring (March to May) brings blossom in the Imlil valley and mild weather on the coast. Summer is a good time for this route, since Imlil and Essaouira are much cooler than Marrakech. Autumn is pleasant everywhere. In winter the mountains can be snowy and nights cold, while Essaouira stays mild.

faq.question: Is this tour suitable for families with children?
faq.answer: Yes. Drives are short, the mountain walk can be adapted, and children usually love the mules, the streams and the beach in Essaouira. Tell us the ages of your children when you book, and we'll suggest the right walk and the best rooms.

faq.question: Can we start or finish at Marrakech airport?
faq.answer: Yes. We can pick you up at Marrakech Menara airport on day 1 and drop you there on day 4 instead of at your hotel. On the last day you're back in Marrakech in the late afternoon, so an evening flight works well.

faq.question: Are entrance fees included?
faq.answer: No. Entrance fees for the Bahia Palace, the Saadian Tombs and the Majorelle Garden are paid on the spot and are usually modest. Bring some dirhams in cash; card payment isn't always possible.

faq.question: Can we add a night or change the order?
faq.answer: Yes. As a private tour, it's easy to adapt: add a second night in Essaouira or Imlil, add a day trip to the Ourika valley or the Agafay desert, or start with Essaouira instead. Contact us before or after booking and we'll adjust the plan and the price.

faq.question: What is Essaouira like compared with Marrakech?
faq.answer: Much calmer. Essaouira is a small, walkable port town with a UNESCO-listed medina of white walls and blue shutters, sea ramparts and a long sandy beach. Sellers are relaxed, the air is fresh thanks to the Atlantic wind, and the pace is slow. It's a perfect contrast to the energy of Marrakech, and many travellers say it's their favourite place in Morocco.
